questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2y=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+3{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{2}x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}-12{y}^{′}+40y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-12\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+40{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36)-36+40 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -6 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =6\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =6\pm 2\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(6+2\text{i})x})={e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(6+2\text{i})x})={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $3{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is not a solution.

Example: 
                    Finding the General Solution When the Characteristic Equation Has Imaginary Roots
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 25y =0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Assuming $y=e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x}  = \lambda e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2}  = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x} .
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+25{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+25) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-25 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 5\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y = P\cos{5x} + Q\sin{5x}.
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Complex Solutions of a Characteristic Equation
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the equation $y'' + 10y' + 34y  = 0,$ where $y = y(t).$ If $y = e^{\lambda t}$ is a solution, then what is $\lambda?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Assuming $y = e^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}, \qquad y'' = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda t} .
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+10\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+34{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +34) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\lambda^2 + 10\lambda + 34  = 0,
$$

and we can solve it by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +34 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25)-25+34 & =0 \\ (\lambda +5)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda +5)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda +5 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-5\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda = - 5 \pm 3\textrm{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Non-Solutions of a Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $y = y(t)$ satisfies the equation $y'' - 4y' + 85y = 0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?

I. $-2e^{2t}\cos{9t} + 7e^{2t}\sin{9t}$

II. $e^{2t}\cos{9t}+3e^{2t}\sin{3t}$

III. $-6e^{2t}\sin{9t}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Assuming $y = e^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}, \qquad y'' = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda t} .
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda t}+85{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +85) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding characteristic equation is

$$
\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 85 = 0,
$$

and we can solve it by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +85 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+85 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+81 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-81 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 9\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 9\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\lambda = 2 \pm 9 \textrm{i}$ are the complex roots of the characteristic equation, the general solution takes the form

$$
y = e^{2t} \left( P \cos 9t + Q \sin 9t \right).
$$

Finally, we need to determine whether each of the given functions takes the form shown above.

- Function I takes the above form with $P=-2$ and $Q=7.$ So, it is a solution to the given ODE.

- Function II does *not* take the above form. It contains $\sin 3t,$ which is not included in the above form. So, it is *not* a solution to the given ODE.

- Function III takes the above form with $P=0$ and $Q=-6.$ So, it is a solution to the given ODE.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE has **complex roots**. Let's see how to find the solution in this case.

We will solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + 4y =0.
$$

**Step 1:** Find the characteristic equation.

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x},$ we find the derivatives:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \lambda e^{\lambda x}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}^2y}{\textrm{d}x^2} = \lambda^2 e^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting these into the ODE gives the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0\,(\text{since }{e}^{\lambda x}\ne 0).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Solve for the characteristic roots.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

The roots are a *complex conjugate pair*. Since the roots are distinct, the general solution is a linear combination of the corresponding exponentials:

$$
y = Ae^{2\textrm{i}x} + Be^{-2\textrm{i}x}.
$$

On the next slide, we will use *Euler's formula* to convert this into a more useful real-valued form.

$$

**Step 2:** Solve for the characteristic roots.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{-4} \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

y = Ae^{2\textrm{i}x} + Be^{-2\textrm{i}x}.

tutorials.name: Convert the Complex Solution to a Real-Valued Solution
tutorials.problem:
Recall our solution from the previous slide:

$$
y = Ae^{2\textrm{i}x} + Be^{-2\textrm{i}x}.
$$

We use **Euler's formula**, which states 

$$
e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta,
$$

 to rewrite the exponentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are typically solving for a real-world quantity, our final answer must be a real-valued function. For this to be true, the arbitrary constants $A$ and $B$ must be a complex conjugate pair ($B = \overline{A}$). This implies that the following definitions yield *real* constants $P$ and $Q$:

$$
P = A+B \quad \text{and} \quad Q = \textrm{i}(A-B).
$$

This gives the **general real-valued solution**:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y(x) = P\cos{2x} + Q\sin{2x}},
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are arbitrary real constants determined by initial conditions.

So, for example,

$$
y(x) = \cos{2x} - 2\sin{2x},
$$

corresponding to $P=1$ and $Q=-2,$ is a solution of the given differential equation. On the other hand,

$$
y(x) = \cos{2x} + \sin{x}
$$

is *not* a solution because it contains a function $\sin{x},$ which is not included in the above form representing the general solution.

\begin{aligned}y & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are typically solving for a real-world quantity, our final answer must be a real-valued function. For this to be true, the arbitrary constants $A$ and $B$ must be a complex conjugate pair ($B = \overline{A}$). This implies that the following definitions yield *real* constants $P$ and $Q$:

$$
P = A+B \quad \text{and} \quad Q = \textrm{i}(A-B).
$$

This gives the **general real-valued solution**:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y(x) = P\cos{2x} + Q\sin{2x}},
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are arbitrary real constants determined by initial conditions.

So, for example,

$$
y(x) = \cos{2x} - 2\sin{2x},
$$

corresponding to $P=1$ and $Q=-2,$ is a solution of the given differential equation. On the other hand,

$$
y(x) = \cos{2x} + \sin{x}
$$

is *not* a solution because it contains a function $\sin{x},$ which is not included in the above form representing the general solution.

tutorials.name: Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs: Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE may have complex solutions. In such cases, the general solution will initially involve complex exponentials.

For example, suppose that we want to solve the following differential equation:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6 \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 18y =0.
$$

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x}$, we get the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 18 =0.
$$

We can solve this by *completing the square*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +18 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+18 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-9 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

The two complex roots are $\lambda_1 = 3 + 3\textrm{i}$ and $\lambda_2 = 3 - 3\textrm{i}.$

The general solution is therefore

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Next, we will use *Euler's formula* to rewrite this solution in a form that does not involve complex numbers.

tutorials.name: Convert the Complex Solution to a Real-Valued Solution
tutorials.problem:
Recall that our general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{(3 + 3 \textrm{i})x} + Be^{(3 - 3 \textrm{i})x}.
$$

Our goal is to simplify this to find the **real-valued general solution**. We can do this using **Euler's formula**, which states that 

$$
e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos{\theta} + \textrm{i}\sin{\theta}.
$$

First, we use the law of exponents to separate the real and imaginary parts in the exponential:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A{e}^{3x}{e}^{3\text{i}x}+B{e}^{3x}{e}^{-3\text{i}x} \\  & ={e}^{3x}(A{e}^{3\text{i}x}+B{e}^{-3\text{i}x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we apply Euler's formula with $\theta = 3x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{3x}(A(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)) \\  & ={e}^{3x}((A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants, we can define new arbitrary constants $P=A+B$ and $Q=\textrm{i}(A-B).$ The general solution becomes:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y = e^{3x}(P\cos{3 x} + Q\sin{3 x}).}
$$

This is the final form of the solution, written entirely with real-valued functions.

So, for example,

$$
y(x) = e^{3x}(5\cos{3 x} - \sin{3 x}),
$$

corresponding to $P=5$ and $Q=-1,$ is a solution of the given differential equation. On the other hand,

$$
y(x) =  e^{3x}(\cos{5 x} - \sin{3 x})
$$

is *not* a solution because it contains a function $e^{3x}\cos{5x},$ which is not included in the above form representing the general solution.
